l: Selden's prison escape, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
s: Selden’s prison escape brought him to Baskerville Hall while warders were pursuing him. He then hid on the moor until the search had passed, relying on the Barrymores for help.

s: The Barrymores secretly take Selden in, feed him, and care for him because Eliza cannot abandon her younger brother. They continue sending food while he hides on the moor, although they hope each day that he has moved on.

s: The mysterious tall man on the tor appears as a thin figure standing against the moon with his arms folded and head bowed. Watson sees him clearly, but the figure disappears when Watson turns toward Sir Henry; Sir Henry suggests that he may have been a warder.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: Dr. Watson records growing fears about the moor, the spectral hound, the unknown watcher, and the danger surrounding Sir Henry. Barrymore explains that Selden is still being secretly supplied and reveals that Sir Charles went to the gate to meet a woman whose initials were L. L., based on a partially burned letter. Dr. Mortimer identifies L. L. as Laura Lyons of Coombe Tracey, prompting Watson to plan an interview with her. Barrymore also reports that another, non-convict man is hiding in the old stone huts on the moor and may be the stranger Watson has seen.

l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: Dr. Watson uses his diary and recollections to investigate the dangers surrounding Baskerville Hall. He questions Barrymore, identifies Laura Lyons as a possible source of information about Sir Charles’s death, and resolves to investigate both her and the stranger hiding on the moor.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: Sherlock Holmes receives Watson’s reports from the moor, including the information about the woman identified by the initials L. L. Watson expects this new clue to renew Holmes’s interest and perhaps bring him to Devonshire.

l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: Sir Henry is shaken by the sound on the moor and argues that Selden remains a danger to isolated houses. He agrees not to inform the police about Selden after Barrymore promises that the convict will soon be sent to South America, and he becomes interested in tracing the woman identified as L. L.

l: Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: Barrymore asks Sir Henry not to report Selden because he believes Selden will leave for South America and fears that his capture would harm Barrymore’s wife. He reveals that Sir Charles received a letter from a woman with the initials L. L. and had gone to the gate to meet her, and he later tells Watson that another man is hiding on the moor.

l: Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: Selden remains hidden on the moor and is being supplied with food and provisions by Barrymore. He told Barrymore that another, apparently non-convict man was also hiding there and had a boy bringing him supplies.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: Sir Charles’s death is connected to a meeting he arranged at the gate with a woman whose initials were L. L. Barrymore learned this from a partially burned letter found in Sir Charles’s study after the inquest.

l: Dr. Mortimer, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: Dr. Mortimer gives Watson a lift from the moor and identifies Laura Lyons as the local woman whose initials are L. L. He explains that she is Frankland’s daughter, lives in Coombe Tracey, and was helped by several people, including Sir Charles, to establish a typewriting business.

l: Mrs. Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: Laura Lyons is identified as the woman whose initials match L. L. She lives in Coombe Tracey, is Frankland’s estranged daughter, and may possess information capable of clarifying an incident in the mystery surrounding Sir Charles’s death.

l: the lurking man on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: The stranger on the moor is a tall, thin figure whom Watson saw watching from a tor. Barrymore reports that Selden had seen another apparently gentlemanly man hiding among the old stone huts, suggesting that this stranger is still watching and waiting.

l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: Baskerville Hall is surrounded by fog, rain, and the bleak moor, contributing to the atmosphere of danger. It is the home of Sir Henry and is repeatedly connected with the threats posed by Selden, the stranger, and the unexplained noises.

l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: The moor is described as cold, rain-soaked, foggy, and increasingly dangerous, with the firm uplands becoming a morass. It conceals Selden and another unidentified man, and its noises and apparent watchers continue to trouble Watson and the household.

l: Coombe Tracey, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: Coombe Tracey is the place from which the letter signed with the initials L. L. was sent. It is also where Laura Lyons lives and where the hidden stranger may obtain supplies.

l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: The spectral hound remains an explanation considered for the reports of a strange creature and the repeated baying heard on the moor. Watson rejects the supernatural interpretation but admits that even the idea of a real large hound raises difficult questions.

l: diary (Dr. Watson's diary), The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: Watson’s diary preserves his observations for October 16 and 17, including the weather, his fears, Barrymore’s revelations, and his conversation with Dr. Mortimer. He uses it to continue his narrative after abandoning his earlier method of quoting reports sent to Holmes.

l: the supernatural hound legend, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: The family legend is cited as having been fulfilled by the death of the last occupant of Baskerville Hall. Its apparent connection with Sir Charles’s death contributes to Watson’s sense that a sinister influence surrounds the family.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: Sir Charles’s death becomes more mysterious when Barrymore reveals that he had gone to the gate to meet a woman. A burned letter bearing the initials L. L. suggests that locating this woman could provide important facts about the death.

l: the chase of Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: The chase of Selden has ended without his capture, and Barrymore argues that pursuing him was unfair after the household learned his secret. Sir Henry ultimately agrees not to notify the police while Barrymore arranges for Selden to escape to South America.

l: the letter from Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: The letter from Laura Lyons is not identified by a full name in the surviving fragment, but it was sent from Coombe Tracey in a woman’s hand and signed with the initials L. L. It asked Sir Charles to burn the letter and meet the writer at the gate by ten o’clock.

l: the warning letter to Sir Henry, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 10.
s: The warning letter to Sir Henry is cited as evidence of human agency in London. Watson notes that it may have been written by either a protecting friend or an enemy, and he wonders whether its writer is connected to the stranger on the moor.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
s: The narrator travels to Coombe Tracey to interrogate Mrs. Laura Lyons about her connection with Sir Charles Baskerville. Mrs. Lyons admits that she wrote to Sir Charles asking him to meet her at the garden gate at ten o’clock on the day he died, but insists that she never kept the appointment. She explains that she sought his financial help to regain her freedom from her husband, but received help from another source before the meeting. The narrator remains doubtful of her complete innocence and turns his attention to the clue concerning the lurking man among the stone huts on the moor.

l: Mrs. Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
s: Mrs. Laura Lyons is questioned about her relationship with Sir Charles Baskerville and initially denies writing to him on the day of his death. She later admits that she wrote asking him to meet her, explaining that she wanted financial help with expenses connected to regaining her freedom from her husband. She insists that she never went to the appointment because she received help from another source, though the narrator suspects that she is withholding part of the truth.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
s: Sir Charles Baskerville had helped Mrs. Laura Lyons financially and was asked by her to meet her at the garden gate. He burned her letter, although part of it remained legible. He died at the place and hour at which Mrs. Lyons had arranged to meet him.

l: Coombe Tracey, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
s: Coombe Tracey is where Mrs. Laura Lyons lives and where the narrator goes to question her. The narrator finds her rooms centrally located and well appointed.

l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
s: The moor contains the clue to the identity or whereabouts of the lurking man. After the inconclusive interview with Mrs. Laura Lyons, the narrator decides to return to that line of investigation.

l: the stone huts, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
s: The stone huts on the hillside are believed to be the place where the lurking man on the moor can be found. They become the narrator’s next focus after he is unable to resolve the questions surrounding Mrs. Laura Lyons.

l: the letter from Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
s: Mrs. Laura Lyons's letter asked Sir Charles Baskerville to meet her at the gate by ten o’clock and urged him to burn it. She says that she wrote it to seek his help with expenses connected to her effort to regain her freedom from her husband. Sir Charles burned the letter, but part of it remained legible.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
s: Sir Charles Baskerville's death occurred at the same place and hour at which Mrs. Laura Lyons had asked him to meet her. Mrs. Lyons says that she learned of his death in the newspaper the next morning.

l: the appointment between Mrs. Laura Lyons and Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
s: Mrs. Laura Lyons arranged to meet Sir Charles Baskerville at the garden gate at ten o’clock on the day he died. She acknowledges making the appointment but denies attending it, saying that something intervened and that she received help from another source.

l: the interrogation of Mrs. Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
s: The narrator interrogates Mrs. Laura Lyons about her letters, meetings, and appointment with Sir Charles Baskerville. Under questioning, she changes from denying the letter to admitting that she wrote it, but she refuses to explain what prevented her from keeping the appointment. The interrogation leaves the narrator baffled and convinced that she may still be concealing information.

l: the lurking man on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 11.
s: The narrator has established that the lurking man on the moor is to be sought among the stone huts on the hillside. After questioning Mrs. Laura Lyons without reaching a conclusion, he turns back to investigating this man.

s: Dr. Watson follows a boy across the moor after Mr. Frankland observes him carrying food toward a remote hill. Watson finds an occupied abandoned hut containing supplies and a written report that he has gone to Coombe Tracey. The message convinces Watson that the stranger has been monitoring him through an agent, possibly the boy. Watson waits in the hut, where the stranger eventually arrives and addresses him in a familiar voice.

l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
s: Dr. Watson learns from Mr. Frankland about the boy carrying food across the moor and follows him to an abandoned hut. He finds evidence that the stranger has been tracking him, then hides in the hut and waits for its tenant, who addresses him as Watson.

l: Mr. Frankland, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
s: Mr. Frankland tells Dr. Watson that he has seen a boy carrying a bundle toward a stony hill and believes the boy is taking food to the convict. He shows Watson the boy through his telescope but refuses to inform the police.

l: the lurking man on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
s: The stranger lives in an abandoned hut on the moor and receives food brought by the boy. He has apparently arranged for Watson's movements to be observed and reported, and he eventually comes to the hut and speaks to Watson.

l: Cartwright, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
s: The boy repeatedly carries a bundle along the moor, apparently bringing food to the stranger. He is seen by Mr. Frankland through a telescope and may also be acting as the stranger's agent by reporting Watson's movements.

l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
s: The moor contains many abandoned huts and is described as lonely, barren, and difficult to search. Watson crosses it to reach the hill and the hut where the stranger lives.

l: Black Tor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
s: Black Tor is the place where Watson previously saw the stranger standing. Watson treats it as the centre of his search, and Mr. Frankland points it out while identifying the stony hill beyond it.

l: Coombe Tracey, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
s: Coombe Tracey is named in the written report found in the hut: “Dr. Watson has gone to Coombe Tracey.”

l: the stone huts, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
s: The moor contains many hundreds of abandoned huts. Watson finds one that has been used as a habitation, with blankets, a fire, cooking utensils, water, food tins, and spirits inside.

l: the inquiry into the stranger, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
s: The inquiry has repeatedly been obstructed by bad luck, but Watson gains a promising lead through Mr. Frankland's observation of the boy. Watson discovers that the stranger's hiding place contains evidence of his identity or intentions only in the form of surveillance reports.

l: the stranger's surveillance, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
s: The stranger's surveillance includes monitoring Watson's movements and recording that he has gone to Coombe Tracey. Watson suspects that the boy, or another agent, has reported nearly every step he has taken on the moor.

l: the written message, The Hound of the Baskervilles, And that was a most vague direction. I realised it as I drove
s: The written message is a roughly scrawled pencil note reading, “Dr. Watson has gone to Coombe Tracey.” Watson finds it beneath the boy's bundle in the stranger's hut and interprets it as a report on his movements.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
s: Dr. John Watson discovers that Sherlock Holmes has been secretly living in a hut on the moor while investigating the danger surrounding Sir Henry Baskerville. Holmes explains that he concealed his presence to avoid alerting their opponents and praises Watson’s reports and investigation of Mrs. Laura Lyons in Coombe Tracey. Holmes reveals that Miss Stapleton is actually Jack Stapleton’s wife and that Stapleton has deceived Mrs. Laura Lyons, who expected to marry him after divorcing her husband. Holmes concludes that the matter involves a deliberate murder plot against Sir Henry and warns Watson to guard him closely until the case is complete.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
s: Sherlock Holmes has been secretly living in a hut on the moor with assistance from Cartwright while investigating the case. He tells Dr. John Watson that Miss Stapleton is Jack Stapleton’s wife, identifies Stapleton as their enemy, and says that the murder plot is deliberate and directed against Sir Henry Baskerville.

l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
s: Dr. John Watson finds Sherlock Holmes in the hut after tracking the investigation and initially mistaking him for a criminal. He reports his conversation with Mrs. Laura Lyons, learns Holmes’s reasons for concealing himself, and is instructed to guard Sir Henry Baskerville closely.

l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
s: Sir Henry Baskerville is identified as the intended target of the murder plot. Sherlock Holmes warns Dr. John Watson that Stapleton may strike against him before the investigation is complete.

l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
s: Jack Stapleton is identified by Sherlock Holmes as the enemy behind the danger to Sir Henry Baskerville. Holmes learns that Stapleton is married to Miss Stapleton but presents her as his sister, and he suspects Stapleton of planning a cold-blooded murder.

l: Mrs. Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
s: Miss Stapleton is revealed by Sherlock Holmes to be Jack Stapleton’s wife rather than his sister. Stapleton has concealed the marriage because she would be more useful to him while appearing to be a free woman.

l: Mrs. Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
s: Mrs. Laura Lyons is questioned by Dr. John Watson in Coombe Tracey, and her conversation helps clarify the case. She has an intimate relationship with Jack Stapleton and, while expecting to become his wife after a projected divorce, does not know that he is already married.

l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
s: The moor is where Sherlock Holmes has maintained a secret retreat in a hut while investigating the case. It is also the setting in which Dr. John Watson searches for information and later meets Holmes at dusk.

l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
s: Baskerville Hall is the place where Dr. John Watson is expected to remain with Sir Henry Baskerville. Sherlock Holmes reminds Watson that his duty requires him not to stay away from the Hall for too long.

l: Coombe Tracey, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
s: Coombe Tracey is where Dr. John Watson goes to interview Mrs. Laura Lyons. Sherlock Holmes says that she is the one person there who might assist them in the case.

l: the hut, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
s: The hut on the moor serves as Sherlock Holmes’s concealed retreat and base of investigation. Dr. John Watson enters it while waiting for its occupant and later shares the hut with Holmes while they discuss their findings.

l: the murder plot against Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
s: The murder plot is described by Sherlock Holmes as refined, cold-blooded, and deliberate. Holmes believes it is directed against Sir Henry Baskerville and fears that Jack Stapleton may act before the evidence is complete.

l: the blackmailing case, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
s: The case concerns the danger surrounding Sir Henry Baskerville and the activities of Jack Stapleton. Sherlock Holmes says that the investigation is nearly complete but requires another day or two and the continued protection of Sir Henry.

l: the intimate relationship between Stapleton and Mrs. Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 12.
s: The intimate relationship between Stapleton and Mrs. Laura Lyons involves meetings, letters, and a complete understanding between them. Mrs. Laura Lyons expected to marry Stapleton after a projected divorce, but Holmes believes she may help them once she learns that Stapleton is already married.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson hear a terrible scream and find a man apparently killed while fleeing the hound on the moor. They initially believe the victim is Sir Henry Baskerville, but discover that the body is Selden, who was wearing Sir Henry’s discarded clothing. Holmes concludes that the hound was attracted by an article of Sir Henry’s clothing, though he remains puzzled about how Selden knew the hound was pursuing him. Stapleton arrives, conceals his alarm, and accepts the explanation that Selden died in an accidental fall.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
s: Sherlock Holmes runs across the moor with Dr. John Watson after hearing screams and initially believes Sir Henry Baskerville has been killed. He is relieved to discover that the victim is Selden, then reasons that the hound was drawn by Sir Henry’s clothing. Holmes conceals his suspicions from Stapleton and says that the investigation has not been satisfactory.

l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes across the moor after hearing the screams and helps examine the body. He initially believes that Sir Henry Baskerville is dead and blames himself for leaving him exposed to danger, but then recognizes that the victim is Selden wearing Sir Henry’s clothing. Watson explains to Holmes how the clothing reached Selden.

l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
s: Sir Henry Baskerville is initially believed to be the man killed on the moor. It is learned that his discarded boots, shirt, cap, and other clothing had been passed to Selden, whose wearing of them apparently caused the hound to pursue him.

l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
s: Stapleton approaches Holmes and Dr. John Watson after hearing the cries and seeing the body. He is visibly shocked and disappointed when he learns that the victim is Selden rather than Sir Henry Baskerville, but he conceals his reaction and supports the explanation that Selden died from exposure, madness, and a fall. He asks whether Holmes and Watson heard anything besides a cry, including evidence of the supposed phantom hound.

l: Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
s: Selden, the escaped convict, is the victim found on the moor. He had been wearing clothing formerly belonging to Sir Henry Baskerville and was apparently pursued by the hound before falling over rocks and breaking his neck.

l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
s: The hound is heard as a deep, menacing rumble accompanying Selden’s screams. Holmes concludes that it was released and attracted to an article of Sir Henry Baskerville’s clothing, probably the boot taken from the hotel, and that it pursued Selden to his death.

l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
s: The moor is the dark, desolate setting where the screams are heard and Selden’s body is found. Its broken ground, rocks, cliffs, slopes, and gorse make the search difficult and contribute to the danger of the pursuit.

l: the death of the escaped convict, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
s: Selden dies after fleeing across the moor while apparently pursued by the hound. He falls over rocks and breaks his neck, and his body is found with his skull crushed and blood pooling beneath it.

l: the hound's attack, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
s: The hound's attack is heard through Selden’s terrified screams and the accompanying deep rumble. The pursuit drives Selden across the moor until he falls over a cliff or rocky slope, although the text does not establish that the hound physically reaches him.

l: the investigation, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
s: The investigation appears to have failed when Holmes and Dr. John Watson initially believe that Sir Henry Baskerville has been killed. After identifying Selden, Holmes recognizes that the clothing provides a connection between the hound and Sir Henry, but he continues to insist that the case requires proof rather than conjecture.

l: the supernatural hound legend, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
s: The supernatural hound legend is discussed when Stapleton asks whether Holmes and Dr. John Watson heard evidence of a phantom hound. Holmes and Watson deny hearing anything beyond the cries, while the hound’s actual existence remains unproven in their stated evidence.

l: the old wardrobe (Sir Henry's), The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
s: Sir Henry Baskerville’s old wardrobe had been given to Barrymore, who passed it on to Selden to help him escape. Selden was wearing Sir Henry’s boots, shirt, cap, and other clothing when he died, and Holmes believes the hound followed the scent of one of these items.

l: the body, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A terrible scream—a prolonged yell of horror and anguish—burst
s: The body is first mistaken for Sir Henry Baskerville because it wears Sir Henry’s distinctive ruddy tweed suit. Holmes and Dr. John Watson discover that it is Selden, lying face down in a grotesque position with a crushed skull, and leave it covered on the moor until morning.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
s: Sherlock Holmes tells Dr. Watson that they are finally in close conflict with a highly capable criminal after the wrong man was killed by the criminal’s plot. Holmes says they cannot arrest the man because they lack evidence connecting him to the hound or to the deaths, and he hopes Mrs. Laura Lyons and his own plan will help establish a case. Holmes intends to conceal the hound from Sir Henry and asks Dr. Watson to avoid a dinner with Stapleton so that Sir Henry will face the ordeal alone.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
s: Sherlock Holmes believes the criminal is an exceptionally worthy opponent and may respond to being discovered by becoming more cautious or taking desperate measures. He refuses to arrest him without proof and plans to use Mrs. Laura Lyons and his own investigation to establish a case. He tells Dr. Watson to conceal the hound from Sir Henry and to excuse himself from the planned dinner.

l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
s: Dr. Watson urges Holmes to arrest the suspected criminal and argues that there is a case based on Sir Charles’s death. He reports that he is engaged to dine with the people the next day, but Holmes instructs him to excuse himself so Sir Henry will attend alone.

l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
s: Stapleton has seen Sherlock Holmes, and Holmes believes this may alter his plans. Stapleton would have Sir Henry believe that Selden’s death had the explanation he provided.

l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
s: The hound is believed by Holmes and Dr. Watson to have frightened Sir Charles to death and to have been involved in the other man’s death, but they have never seen it. They heard it, yet cannot prove that it was following the dead man’s trail, and Holmes says there are no visible marks or other direct evidence connecting it to the deaths.

l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
s: Sir Henry is expected to dine with Stapleton and the others the next day. Holmes wants him kept unaware of the hound so that he will have a better nerve for the ordeal and will attend the dinner alone.

l: Mrs. Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
s: Sherlock Holmes has great hopes that Mrs. Laura Lyons will help once the position of affairs is made clear to her.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
s: Sir Charles was found dead without any mark upon him. Holmes and Dr. Watson believe that he died of sheer fright caused by the hound, but Holmes says they cannot prove this explanation to a jury.

l: the death of the escaped convict, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
s: Selden’s death is described as another death with no direct connection yet proven between the hound and the victim’s death. Holmes tells Dr. Watson to let Sir Henry think that Selden’s death occurred as Stapleton would have him believe.

l: the trial case against Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, “We’re at close grips at last,” said Holmes as we walked together
s: Holmes says there is currently no trial case against Stapleton, only surmise and conjecture. The evidence does not directly connect him to the hound or the deaths, so Holmes believes they must risk further investigation to establish a case.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.
s: Sherlock Holmes identifies Mr. Stapleton as a Baskerville descendant by comparing his face with the portrait of Hugo Baskerville and plans to trap him. Holmes arranges for Sir Henry Baskerville to visit the Stapletons and walk home alone while Holmes and Dr. Watson secretly return with Inspector Lestrade. Mrs. Laura Lyons reveals that Stapleton dictated her letter to Sir Charles Baskerville, deceived her about his marriage, and persuaded her not to keep her appointment with Sir Charles. Holmes believes the evidence against Stapleton is nearing completion, though he intends to gather further proof before arresting him.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 13.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The document is *The Hound of the Baskervilles*, presented as an adventure of Sherlock Holmes by A. Conan Doyle, inspired by a West-Country legend. It follows Holmes, Dr. John Watson, Sir Henry Baskerville, and Dr. James Mortimer as they investigate the apparent supernatural curse surrounding the Baskerville family. In London, Holmes and Watson first deduce facts about Mortimer from his walking stick. Mortimer then brings the Baskerville legend and evidence about Sir Charles Baskerville’s unexplained death: the frightened man died near the moor, with gigantic hound-like footprints nearby. Sir Henry, the new heir, receives an anonymous warning to avoid the moor, loses boots under suspicious circumstances, and is followed by a disguised spy. Although Holmes investigates the London clues, he sends Watson with Sir Henry to Baskerville Hall in Devonshire. Watson reports from the moor, where escaped murderer Selden, the secretive Barrymores, strange cries, and the dangerous Grimpen Mire deepen the mystery. He meets Jack Stapleton and Beryl Stapleton; Beryl warns that Sir Henry should leave, while Sir Henry becomes attached to her. Watson learns that the Barrymores are aiding Selden, that Sir Charles had arranged to meet Laura Lyons, and that an unknown man watches from the moor. The watcher proves to be Holmes, secretly investigating from a stone hut. Holmes concludes that Stapleton, whose supposed sister is actually his wife, is conducting a deliberate plot against Sir Henry. Stapleton has manipulated Laura Lyons and used the Baskerville legend to terrorize and kill Sir Charles. Selden is killed after wearing Sir Henry’s discarded clothes and being pursued by the hound. Holmes then identifies Stapleton as a concealed Baskerville descendant seeking the estate. Holmes, Watson, and Inspector Lestrade set a trap when Sir Henry visits Merripit House. Stapleton releases a huge black hound, made fiery-looking with phosphorus, but Holmes and Watson shoot it before it kills Sir Henry. They free the abused Mrs. Stapleton, while Stapleton flees toward the Grimpen Mire. Evidence at the hound’s hiding place, including Sir Henry’s missing boot, suggests that Stapleton was swallowed by the mire. Holmes finally explains that Stapleton used the painted hound, the family curse, deception, and fear to eliminate the heirs and inherit Baskerville property; Mrs. Stapleton ultimately tried to warn Sir Henry.

It follows an adventure featuring Sherlock Holmes through a Baskerville curse and problem involving Sir Henry Baskerville, Baskerville Hall, the Stapletons of Merripit House, and the moor. l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Sherlock Holmes is the central figure of the Baskerville adventure: a London-based consulting detective, specialist in crime and scientific deduction, and friend and companion of Dr. John Watson. Clear, alert, professionally cautious, and able to detach his mind at will, he uses close observation, maps, printed matter, portraits, reports, and concealed surveillance to investigate Sir Charles Baskerville’s death and protect Sir Henry Baskerville. He begins by deducing facts from Dr. James Mortimer’s stick, dating and assessing a manuscript, questioning Mortimer about the death, and examining the warning letter. His inquiries identify surveillance of Sir Henry, but several London leads fail, so he sends Watson to Devonshire with strict instructions to report facts, stay with Sir Henry, and keep him from the moor alone. Although occupied by other cases, Holmes secretly travels to the moor, lives in a hut with Cartwright’s help, receives Watson’s delayed reports, and investigates from Coombe Tracey. He identifies Miss Stapleton as Jack Stapleton’s wife, recognizes Stapleton as the enemy and a Baskerville through a portrait, and concludes that Sir Charles died of fright caused by a hound. Refusing to arrest Stapleton on conjecture, Holmes gathers proof through Mrs. Laura Lyons and arranges a trap using Sir Henry. During the ambush he shoots the hound, rescues Sir Henry, finds Mrs. Stapleton, and follows Stapleton’s route into the Grimpen Mire, where he explains the missing boot, the hound’s confinement and luminous coating, and Stapleton’s deception. He ends by reconstructing the mystery from testimony and notes, having exposed the deliberate plot against Sir Henry.

l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Dr. Watson is a medical doctor, M.R.C.S., narrator, and Sherlock Holmes’s friend, companion, assistant, and reporter of facts. The records follow his role in the Baskerville inquiry from London to Devonshire. At first, he joins Holmes in examining Dr. Mortimer’s evidence, makes some mistaken deductions about Mortimer’s stick, and listens to the account of Sir Charles Baskerville’s death and the Baskerville legend. When Sir Henry appears to be threatened, Watson agrees to accompany him to Baskerville Hall as Holmes’s agent, with orders to protect him, keep a revolver close, and send full written reports. In Devonshire, Watson observes the household and moor, investigates Barrymore’s movements, questions local people, meets Jack and Beryl Stapleton, hears the hound’s cry, and records his suspicions and discoveries in reports and a diary. He remains concerned for Sir Henry’s safety, though he sometimes acts beyond Holmes’s instructions, including following Sir Henry onto the moor. He and Sir Henry uncover the Barrymores’ secret, pursue Selden, and see an unidentified man on a tor. Watson then investigates Laura Lyons and the stranger supplied by a boy, only to discover that the stranger is Holmes, who has concealed his presence and has been using Watson’s reports. As the danger closes in, Watson feels responsible when Selden, dressed in Sir Henry’s clothing, is killed. He presses Holmes to act against the suspected criminal. In the final confrontation, Watson watches Stapleton and Sir Henry, joins Holmes in pursuing the hound, fires at it, helps rescue Sir Henry and Mrs. Stapleton, and later helps Holmes escape the Grimpen Mire. At the end, he discusses Holmes’s explanation of the case and is invited away from the severe work to attend Les Huguenots and dine at Marcini’s.

l: the Baskerville family, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The Baskerville family is an old, masterful line rooted in Baskerville Hall, where it has lived for five hundred years and which it has owned through its caretakers for four generations. Its identity is dominated by a hereditary legend: since the death of its ancestor Hugo Baskerville, a supernatural or demonic hound is said to have plagued the family, with many members suffering sudden, bloody, mysterious deaths. The hall’s portraits and coats of arms preserve the family’s long presence, while the legend remains a serious superstition for Sir Charles and a childhood story for Sir Henry. After Sir Charles’s death, Sir Henry inherits the estate as the last surviving representative, seeking to keep the title, house, land, and money together; the distant Desmond cousins would succeed if he died. Rodger Baskerville, the family’s black sheep, died in Central America in 1876, and the later account identifies Stapleton as connected to the family through Rodger.
