l: the legend of the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The legend of the Hound of the Baskervilles is a family curse story about a dreadful, demonic hound said to haunt the Baskervilles. It begins with Hugo Baskerville pursuing an abducted maiden across the moor and being killed by a monstrous hound; the legend then claims the creature caused sudden, bloody, mysterious deaths among family members. It deeply affects Sir Charles and creates fear that Sir Henry faces the same dark fate. Dr. Mortimer and witnesses connect marks near Sir Charles’s body and an apparition to the legend, while local discussion and Stapleton’s guarded comments sustain belief in an evil family influence. In the end, Stapleton exploits Sir Charles’s superstition and reports involving the hound to conceal human responsibility for Sir Charles’s death.

l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Sir Henry Baskerville is the young baronet, nephew and heir of Sir Charles Baskerville, the last representative of the Baskerville family, and inheritor of the Baskerville estate, title, Hall, and seven hundred and forty thousand pounds. Formerly farming in Canada and spending much of his time in America and Canada, he arrives in England to claim his inheritance. In London, after a warning to keep away from the moor and the strange theft and return of his boots, he insists on visiting Baskerville Hall despite danger. An unknown pursuer shadows him, and he asks Dr. John Watson to accompany him to Devonshire. At Baskerville Hall, Sir Henry is both eager to improve the place, including with electric lamps, and unsettled by its atmosphere and the moor. He investigates local concerns with Watson, confronts Barrymore over a telegram, learns the Barrymores have aided Selden, and is alarmed by the cry believed to be the Hound of the Baskervilles. He becomes strongly attracted to Miss Stapleton, proposes marriage, quarrels with Stapleton, and agrees to wait three months while remaining her friend, unaware that she is Stapleton's wife. Sir Henry is the intended victim of Stapleton's plot to gain the estate. Selden is first mistaken for him after wearing Sir Henry's discarded clothing, which draws the hound. Holmes then has Sir Henry dine with the Stapletons and walk home alone as bait to expose Stapleton. The hound attacks Sir Henry on the moor, but Holmes and the others rescue him before he is wounded. He is brought back to Baskerville Hall with a high fever and severe shock, though the doctors expect his illness to be temporary.

l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Baskerville Hall is an ancient manor house and family home in Devonshire, the ancestral seat and residence of the Baskerville family. Set near the moor and yew alley and surrounded by wood, it has ivy-covered granite walls, twin ancient towers, a dark avenue, a large heavily timbered hall, and a second-floor western lattice window with the nearest outlook onto the moor. Sir Charles lived there and took his final nightly walk from the yew alley; its grim reputation and the danger feared for a Baskerville make occupancy uncertain. After inheriting, Sir Henry resolves to return despite warnings, arriving with Dr. John Watson to be received by Barrymore and his wife. The Hall initially seems gloomy, though morning sunlight makes it appear less so. Its nights remain troubled by a woman crying, unexplained sobbing, suspicions about Barrymore, secret business, and threats associated with the escaped Selden, a stranger, noises, fog, rain, and the surrounding moor. Barrymore and his wife use the Hall to signal Selden by candle and provide him food. While Sir Henry lives there with Watson, he plans extensive renovation and refurnishing to restore its grandeur; Stapleton believes an inhabited Hall would benefit poor people on the moor. Watson is expected to remain with Sir Henry, but after later night events Holmes and Watson bring Sir Henry back feverish and delirious for Dr. Mortimer’s care. The Hall’s history is finally tied to Stapleton, who established himself nearby and arranged the circumstances of Sir Charles’s death as Sir Charles prepared to leave on medical advice.

l: Merripit House, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Merripit House is Stapleton’s house near the moor, home to Jack and Beryl Stapleton and associated with Miss Stapleton and Mrs. Stapleton. It contains Stapleton’s museum room and is where Jack invites Dr. Watson to meet his sister. Later, Sir Henry and Watson plan to dine there after a quarrel ends. It becomes the scene of Holmes’s ambush and the hound’s attack; afterward, Mrs. Stapleton is found tied up, and Anthony’s role is suspected.

l: diary (Dr. Watson's diary), The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Watson’s diary preserves his observations for October 16 and 17, including the weather, his fears, Barrymore’s revelations, and his conversation with Dr. Mortimer. He uses it to continue his narrative after abandoning his earlier method of quoting reports sent to Holmes.

l: the death of the escaped convict, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Selden dies after fleeing across the moor amid a terrible scream, apparently pursued by the hound. He falls over rocks, breaks his neck, and is found with a crushed skull and blood beneath him. Stapleton attributes the death to the hound, but no direct connection can be proved; Holmes urges Watson to preserve Stapleton’s account for Sir Henry.

l: Dr. Mortimer, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Dr. James Mortimer is a married medical doctor: a country practitioner based in Grimpen, medical officer for Thorsley and High Barrow, and formerly house surgeon at Charing Cross Hospital from 1882 to 1884. A presentation stick given by hospital friends at his marriage marked his departure from the hospital and from hopes of a consulting practice. He is described as a humble M.R.C.S., an unpractical but precise-minded scientific man, a dabbler in science, and learned in his own line. His scientific record includes the Jackson prize for Comparative Pathology, corresponding membership in the Swedish Pathological Society, articles in The Lancet and Journal of Psychology, comparative-anatomical interests in the Bushman and Hottentot, and amateur archaeology, including a prehistoric skull excavated at Long Down. He owns a curly-haired spaniel and is assessed by Sherlock Holmes as entirely honest. Mortimer’s central role concerns Sir Charles Baskerville. As Sir Charles’s personal friend, medical attendant, trustee, executor, and keeper of the Baskerville manuscript, he brings Holmes the manuscript and report of Sir Charles’s death. He recounts Sir Charles’s fear of the family legend, huge hound-like footprints near the body, and reports of a luminous spectral creature, and he entertains the possibility of a Baskerville demon. Concerned for Sir Henry Baskerville, he consults Holmes, brings Sir Henry to Baker Street, explains the inheritance and its succession, and helps frame the warning as possibly supernatural. He receives one thousand pounds under Sir Charles’s will, while also reporting the legacies to Barrymore and Barrymore’s wife. Mortimer travels with Sir Henry and Dr. Watson to Devonshire, delivers them to Baskerville Hall, and returns to his wife. He knows nearly all residents within driving distance, identifies Laura Lyons and the support she received, and reports information about Barrymore, Sir Charles’s weak heart, and Sir Henry’s arrival. He later visits Holmes and Watson with Sir Henry before their intended long voyage, which he advises to restore Sir Henry’s nerves. He is followed from Holmes’s house by a black-bearded spy and remains a companion of Baskerville throughout the affair.

l: Mortimer's presentation stick, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Mortimer’s presentation stick is a thick, bulbous-headed Penang lawyer with a silver band engraved to James Mortimer from friends of the C.C.H., dated 1884. Presented for his marriage, it is worn from extensive walking and marked by his spaniel’s teeth; Mortimer values it enough to return for it.

l: Charing Cross Hospital, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Charing Cross Hospital, located in London, employed Dr. James Mortimer as house-surgeon from 1882 to 1884; friends there gave him a stick on his marriage.

l: London, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: London is a place containing Baker Street and serving as both refuge and field of danger in the investigation around Sir Henry Baskerville. Holmes argues that it cannot guarantee safety from a supernatural force, yet Sir Henry arrives there unfamiliar with British life, shops, receives a warning, and returns to the Northumberland Hotel. The city becomes the setting for surveillance and inquiry, though its size frustrates efforts to identify watchers; Holmes also remains because of his practice and another case. Beryl urges returns to London, and Barrymore’s possible presence there is investigated. Holmes pretends to return there with Watson, sends Cartwright onward, and secretly stays nearby. Stapleton had used London for lodging, disguise, surveillance, and obtaining a boot for the hound.

l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Dartmoor is a sparsely inhabited, desolate moor and plain around Baskerville Hall: a vast, bleak, granite-flecked landscape rolling to the horizon, marked by tors, cairns, boulders, cold wind, prehistoric huts, graves, monoliths, scattered farms and dwellings, and a nearby prison. It contains Grimpen Mire, dangerous bogland; many abandoned stone huts; sheep; Cleft Tor; Stapleton's abode; Selden in hiding; and the recurring strange cry. Its barrenness, broken ground, fog, rain, cliffs, slopes, gorse, and morass make travel, searching, and pursuit difficult and dangerous. From the beginning, it surrounds the Baskerville estate and frames the legend's pursuit and Hugo Baskerville's death. Sir Charles stopped at its gate before his death, where Dr. James Mortimer found footprints of Barrymore and an alleged gigantic hound. It becomes the source of the warning that Sir Henry should keep away, especially after dark, and Dr. Mortimer considers it unsafe for the Baskerville family. As Sir Henry approaches Baskerville Hall, the moor's grey, melancholy, jagged, isolated character intensifies the family's feared danger. It then becomes the setting for exploration, concealment, and surveillance. Stapleton claims extensive knowledge of it; Beryl warns Watson away; Barrymore watches it at night; and the Barrymores secretly supply Selden there. Watson and Sir Henry cross it, hear its frightening cry, and see a tall man on a tor. As weather worsens, it conceals Selden and another unidentified man. Watson searches its lonely huts and discovers that Holmes has used one as a secret retreat. Later, screams are heard, Selden's body is found, and finally the moor provides the fog-bound ground for the ambush, the hound's attack, and the pursuit.

l: scientific deduction, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Scientific deduction is demonstrated through the examination of Mortimer’s stick, its inscription, its wear, and the marks left by a dog. Holmes uses these clues to revise Watson’s mistaken assumptions and infer Mortimer’s profession, history, age, personality, and ownership of a curly-haired spaniel.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Sir Charles Baskerville was a late baronet, wealthy public man, and generous, childless owner of Baskerville Hall and the Baskerville estate. After making his fortune in South African speculation, he restored the Hall and lived there in retirement for the two years before his death. Known for a kind heart, he helped Mrs. Laura Lyons financially, appointed Mr. Stapleton as his almoner on several occasions, and left substantial gifts to Barrymore and his wife, Dr. James Mortimer, charities, and others. His estate, worth close to a million pounds, passed in residue to his next of kin and heir, Sir Henry Baskerville. Sir Charles had long-standing organic heart disease, a weak heart, breathlessness, and nervous depression. Deeply impressed by the curse of the Baskervilles and fearful of the family hound legend, he nevertheless enjoyed walking over the moor. On the day of his death, he received and partly burned a letter from Mrs. Laura Lyons asking him to meet her at the garden or moor-gate at ten o'clock. The appointment had been manipulated. He waited near the gate, then ran in terror down the yew alley toward the moor, where he was found dead near the end of the alley, about fifty yards from the summer-house. Medical evidence gave cardiac exhaustion as the cause, while gigantic hound footprints were reported near his body. Stapleton, whom Sir Charles had befriended and told of the family hound, exploited his weak heart and superstition. He arranged for the hound to pursue and terrify Sir Charles, killing him through heart disease and terror. Sir Charles's death shocked the devoted Barrymores, left the Hall painful to them, and made his will and fortune important to the investigation.

l: Hugo Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Hugo Baskerville, a direct-line ancestor who held Baskerville Hall during the Great Rebellion, was a wild, profane, godless, cruel man and father of Rodger, John, and Elizabeth. Family tradition says he began the Hound story after abducting a yeoman’s daughter, pursuing her, and dying beside her beneath a huge black hound.

l: Mr. Frankland, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Mr. Frankland is an elderly, red-faced, white-haired, choleric landowner, litigant, and amateur astronomer. He treats costly litigation as a habitual amusement, winning a right of way, closing Fernworthy, and suing Sir John Morland. From his telescope he watches the moor, sees a boy carrying food toward a stony hill, suspects aid to the escaped convict, tells Dr. Watson, and refuses police help.

l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Stapleton is a man who appears first as a black-bearded spy falsely claiming to be Sherlock Holmes while following Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Watson. In Devonshire he presents himself as Jack Stapleton, a naturalist, former schoolmaster, and entomological authority living at Merripit House near Baskerville Hall with Beryl, whom he calls his sister. He knows the moor and paths through Grimpen Mire, collects Lepidoptera, and cultivates Sir Charles Baskerville as a friend. His apparent concern over Beryl’s relationship with Sir Henry leads him to confront Sir Henry and later apologize. Holmes uncovers that this identity conceals a calculated criminal. Stapleton is Beryl’s husband, not her brother, and a Baskerville descendant, Rodger Baskerville’s son, whose real name was also Rodger Baskerville; he had also used Vandeleur. Seeking the Baskerville estate, he befriends Sir Charles, manipulates Mrs. Laura Lyons with a promise of marriage, dictates her letter to Sir Charles, and frightens her into silence. He causes Sir Charles’s death through terror and heart disease. Stapleton keeps a hound hidden in an old tin mine on an island in the Grimpen Mire, coats it with a luminous mixture to make it seem supernatural, and uses it to murder or frighten his targets. He plans Sir Henry’s death, using a missing boot to give the hound Sir Henry’s scent. When Selden is killed instead, Stapleton conceals his disappointment and continues the deception. He hosts Sir Henry at Merripit House, releases the hound, and flees after Holmes, Watson, and Lestrade intervene. Carrying Sir Henry’s boot, he attempts to cross the mire to his refuge and is believed to be swallowed by Grimpen Mire. His abandoned refuge exposes the hound, the luminous paste, and his plot.

l: Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Barrymore is the butler and servant in charge of Baskerville Hall, where he lives with his wife, Mrs. or Eliza Barrymore. Tall and handsome with a full black beard, he comes from the former caretaker’s family and says that his family has served the Baskervilles for generations, even over a hundred years. He and his wife were attached to Sir Charles Baskerville, whose body Barrymore first discovered, and they consider leaving the hall because it is painful after Sir Charles’s death. When Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Watson arrive, Barrymore receives them, handles their luggage, offers dinner, and shows them their rooms and the dining room. Yet his black beard, the uncertain telegram delivery, his wife’s concealed crying, and his nighttime movements make him suspicious. Though he says he received the telegram, Mrs. Barrymore brought it to him and wrote his dictated reply. Watson sees him barefoot at night with a candle, watching the moor from a western window. Barrymore is eventually found using the candle as a signal. He admits that he and Eliza have been secretly feeding Selden, her brother and Barrymore’s brother-in-law, while concealing him from the police. He asks Sir Henry not to report Selden, fearing the effect on his wife and believing Selden will leave for South America. Sir Henry permits the couple to remain. Barrymore also reveals that Sir Charles received a letter from L. L. and went to the gate to meet her, and tells Watson that another man is hiding on the moor.

l: Mrs. Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Mrs. Barrymore, also called Eliza Barrymore, is John Barrymore’s wife and a servant at Baskerville Hall. Though described as heavy, solid, puritanical, and respectable, she repeatedly shows deep sorrow through tears. The mystery of her distress ends when she reveals that Selden is her younger brother and that she asked John to help feed and protect him on the moor.

l: the Baskerville estate, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The Baskerville estate is a nearly million-pound property, including securities and a large residue, centred on Baskerville Hall amid lodge-gates, an avenue, and moorland. Entailed to the Desmond family if Sir Henry dies, it is meant by him to remain with the title and property. Beautiful to Sir Henry but melancholy to Dr. Watson, it becomes Stapleton’s target as he seeks to remove the two heirs before him and inherit it.

l: Devonshire, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Devonshire is the county containing Baskerville Hall and a poor countryside whose prosperity depends on the Hall having a tenant. Dr. Mortimer fears Sir Henry Baskerville may meet the Baskerville fate there. Sir Henry, Dr. Watson, and Dr. Mortimer leave London for Devonshire, where Holmes expects better investigative prospects despite danger. Arriving by train, they find greener, damper, rugged country of granite, wooded valleys, and distant moorland; Sir Henry warmly recognizes it.

l: the Baskerville manuscript, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: A 1742 family paper, entrusted by Sir Charles Baskerville to Dr. James Mortimer, recounts Hugo Baskerville’s Hound legend and ends by warning the family against the moor when evil powers are exalted.

l: the Devon County Chronicle, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The Devon County Chronicle published an account of Sir Charles Baskerville's death on May 14th. It reported the evidence from the inquest, including his heart condition, his nightly walk through the yew alley, the absence of physical injury, and the coroner's verdict of natural death.

l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The Hound of the Baskervilles is a gigantic, coal-black hound associated with the Baskerville family and its inherited curse. In the family narrative it is a huge, hellish, diabolical-seeming beast that kills Hugo Baskerville by tearing out his throat; local tradition later treats it as a supernatural creature or phantom that haunts the moor. Its alleged appearance, footprints near Sir Charles Baskerville’s body, and cries on the moor feed fear that the legend is real. Sir Henry, though once dismissive of the tale, becomes alarmed when he and Watson hear a strange cry. Watson rejects a supernatural explanation, while Holmes considers that a real, unusually large hound could account for the reports but lacks direct proof linking it to deaths. The hound is released, follows the scent of Sir Henry’s stolen clothing, and pursues Selden to his death. Holmes and Watson conclude it likely frightened Sir Charles to death as well, though it does not bite dead bodies. The truth is that Stapleton keeps this savage animal chained in an abandoned miners’ cottage on a bog-girt island, using it as his agent. The hound is a gaunt cross between a bloodhound and a mastiff, as large as a small lioness; Stapleton daubs it with a luminous mixture, giving it its phosphorescent, supernatural appearance. It attacks Sir Henry, but Holmes and Watson shoot it repeatedly with revolvers, killing it.

l: the Baskerville curse, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The Baskerville curse is a family belief that a hound has plagued the Baskervilles since Hugo Baskerville's death, bringing evil fates to those who go to Baskerville Hall. Sir Charles and Dr. Mortimer take the threat seriously, especially for Sir Henry, while Holmes withholds belief in a supernatural cause and considers human danger.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Sir Charles Baskerville’s death is the central event of a continuing murder investigation. After taking his customary nightly walk in the yew alley, he was found dead at its far end, without visible injury or mark. Dr. James Mortimer noted terror on his face and fresh footprints of a gigantic hound; other evidence suggested that Sir Charles had waited at the moor-gate before fleeing down the alley. The coroner’s jury attributed the death to cardiac exhaustion, but the unexplained tracks, reports of a spectral creature, and signs of fear left open questions of crime, human agency, and supernatural causes. The death deeply shocked Barrymore and his wife, as well as Beryl and Stapleton, and Beryl believed it strengthened fears about the Baskerville family’s curse. Holmes investigates after Dr. Mortimer’s consultation, while Watson revisits the alley and gate and seeks further particulars. Barrymore reveals that Sir Charles had gone to the gate to meet a woman, and a burned letter leads to Mrs. Laura Lyons. Her appointment, made for the same place and hour and later canceled under Stapleton’s influence, becomes a key connection. Holmes and Watson conclude that Sir Charles died of fright and exhaustion after being pursued by the hound. Stapleton had arranged for him to wait at the gate, released the painted hound, and thereby indirectly caused his death; however, Holmes says the evidence would not prove this to a jury.

l: the yew alley, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The yew alley is a famous avenue on the grounds of Baskerville Hall, bounded by two impenetrable twelve-foot yew hedges, with a central walk, grass strips, a moor-gate, and a summer-house exit. Sir Charles Baskerville habitually walked it before bed; on the night of his death, his footprints changed beyond the moor-gate and ended where he was found after apparently running through the alley.

l: the Baskerville demon, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: A huge, luminous, ghastly, spectral creature, unlike known animals, is repeatedly seen on Dartmoor before Sir Charles Baskerville’s death.

l: Waterloo Station, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: is_in London Waterloo Station is where Dr. Mortimer is due to meet Sir Henry Baskerville after his arrival in England. Holmes directs Mortimer to go there and then bring Sir Henry to Baker Street the following morning.

l: the Baskerville mystery, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The Baskerville mystery is the investigation of Sir Charles Baskerville’s murder and the threat to Sir Henry. Holmes first examines whether a crime occurred, how Sir Charles died, and clues including footprints, movements, the moor-gate, and fear-induced flight. As Stapleton’s family connection and Mrs. Laura Lyons’s testimony emerge, the case becomes connected. It ends with Holmes identifying Stapleton’s scheme to gain the estate by killing both men and disguising it through the hound legend.

l: Northumberland Hotel, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The Northumberland Hotel is a London hotel chosen by Baskerville as his town lodging, where Sir Henry Baskerville stays when his warning letter arrives. Its register is examined by Holmes, who finds no interested parties staying there. The hotel’s importance is that Baskerville’s choice becomes known quickly, indicating he is closely followed by people watching from elsewhere.

l: the warning letter, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The warning letter is a greyish envelope sent to Sir Henry Baskerville at the Northumberland Hotel, posted from Charing Cross. Made from pasted newspaper words and addressed in a disguised hand, it warns him of danger. Mrs. Stapleton created it by cutting out and assembling the message, and it reached Sir Henry as his initial warning.

l: the warning letter to Sir Henry, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: A newspaper-clipping warning letter to Sir Henry tells him to keep away from the moor if he values his life or reason. Its pasted printed words, except “moor,” conceal the sender’s identity. Later it is evidence of human agency in London, possibly from either a protector or an enemy.

l: The Times, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: has_center_page cut-out center page of The Times [the page sought among hotel waste-paper] Holmes gives Cartwright a copy of The Times and identifies the page he must search for in hotel waste-paper. The page is the center page, marked by holes cut with scissors.

l: the inheritance, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Sir Henry has inherited the Baskerville family estate after his uncle’s death. He says that he has come into the inheritance “with a vengeance” and must decide whether to proceed to Baskerville Hall.

l: the danger on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The danger on the moor concerns Sir Henry’s planned journey to Baskerville Hall, where danger may be supernatural or human. Holmes thinks a warning either protects him or frightens him away for another purpose. Beryl says living there has been fatal to his family but cannot identify the danger. Miss Stapleton repeatedly urges him to leave, but Sir Henry stays after meeting her.

l: the planned journey to Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: is_intended_by Sir Henry Baskerville [despite warnings] The planned journey to Baskerville Hall is the main practical decision facing Sir Henry. Despite warnings of possible supernatural or human danger, he firmly decides that he will go and asks for time to think before giving Holmes and Dr. Watson his final view.

l: the newspaper clipping message, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: A message assembled from words cut from The Times’s leading article on free trade and pasted onto foolscap. Holmes identifies its source by type, notes two phrases were cut together, and explains that “moor” was handwritten because unavailable in print.

l: unknown pursuer (Baskerville's shadow), The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: An unknown pursuer follows Baskerville through town in hansom cab No. 2704, apparently concealing himself with a likely false bushy black beard. After detecting Holmes and Watson, he escapes, ending their chance to observe him.

l: Cartwright, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Cartwright is a fourteen-year-old district messenger with a bright, keen face. Holmes sends him to search waste-paper at twenty-three nearby hotels for a cut-up center page of The Times, but he fails to find it. Later, disguised as a country boy, he assists Sherlock Holmes on the moor, supplying bread and clean collars and observing events. He follows a daily path carrying food to the stranger, and Mr. Frankland sees him through a telescope; he may report Watson’s movements.

l: Baker Street, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Baker Street is Sherlock Holmes's residence and the place to which Holmes and Dr. Watson return after meeting Sir Henry. John Clayton comes there to answer Holmes's questions about the cab passenger who followed them.

l: hansom cab No. 2704, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: has_number 2704 Hansom cab No. 2704 carries the unknown pursuer as he follows Baskerville. The pursuer escapes in it after seeing Holmes and Watson, and Holmes intends to discover the identity of its cabman by wire.

l: the twenty-three nearby hotels, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Twenty-three hotels near Charing Cross are listed in the Hotel Directory; Cartwright is instructed to visit each and inspect the previous day’s waste-paper.

l: cut-out center page of The Times, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: has_holes_cut_in_it scissors The cut-out center page of The Times is the object Holmes wants Cartwright to find. Cartwright is told to recognize it by comparing it with the copy Holmes provides.

l: waste-paper from the hotels, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Waste-paper from the hotels may contain the cut-out center page of The Times. In most hotels, paper from the day before is removed or burned; only about three may retain heaps available for searching.

l: Baskerville's shadowing, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: is_conducted_by unknown pursuer (Baskerville's shadow) [closely, since Baskerville has been in town] Baskerville's shadowing is revealed by the pursuer's rapid knowledge of Baskerville's hotel and continued following through London. Holmes believes the pursuer used a cab to remain hidden, follow or pass Baskerville, and be ready to follow if Baskerville hired a cab.

l: Holmes and Watson's pursuit, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: targets unknown pursuer (Baskerville's shadow) [to identify or follow him] Holmes and Watson follow Dr. Mortimer and Baskerville while trying to identify Baskerville's invisible attendant. They approach the pursuer's cab, but the pursuer recognizes them and escapes before they can obtain more than the cab number.

l: Cartwright's hotel investigation, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Cartwright visits twenty-three nearby hotels, paying outside and hall porters while searching waste-paper for the cut-out center page of The Times; Holmes provides emergency money and requires a wire report to Baker Street before evening.

l: Sir Henry's missing boots, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: A series of unexplained incidents begins when one of Sir Henry Baskerville's new brown boots disappears, then an old black boot is lost from the hotel; the brown boot is later found under a cabinet without explanation.

l: the letter from Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Laura Lyons’s partially burned letter, sent from Coombe Tracey in a woman’s hand and signed L. L., asks Sir Charles Baskerville to burn it and meet her at the gate by ten o’clock. She wrote to seek his help with expenses for regaining freedom from her husband. Sir Charles burned it, though a fragment remained legible.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville's will, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Sir Charles Baskerville's will gives five hundred pounds each to Barrymore and Mrs. Barrymore, one thousand to Dr. Mortimer, smaller sums to others, and its seven hundred and forty thousand pound residue to Sir Henry Baskerville, raising inheritance and motive questions if Sir Henry dies.

l: the surveillance of Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: occurs_in London The surveillance of Sir Henry Baskerville continues in London through watchers who stay at hotels other than the Northumberland Hotel. A black-bearded man follows Sir Henry and Dr. Watson, but his identity and purpose remain unknown after he deceives Holmes through the cabman.

l: the investigation, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The investigation seeks proof linking a man to the hound threatening Sir Henry Baskerville. Holmes pursues hotel records, missing boots, Barrymore, the will, and a spy’s cabman, but loses several leads and awaits Watson in Devonshire. It seems to fail after a scream and an apparent killing, until the victim is identified as Selden and clothing links the hound to Sir Henry.

l: Barrymore couple, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The Barrymore couple are Baskerville Hall’s household servants, long connected to the Baskerville family and Sir Charles. After Sir Charles’s death, painful memories make them consider leaving; Holmes keeps them among the suspects until their innocence or guilt is determined.

l: Mrs. Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Mrs. Stapleton is the woman living at Merripit House on the moor with Jack Stapleton, publicly presented as his sister but later revealed to be his wife. Beautiful, fascinating, tropical, and exotic in appearance, she is devoted to Nature and shares books and intimate knowledge of Sir Charles with Stapleton. Despite this household connection, she fears Stapleton and becomes a victim of his deception and ill-treatment. She first approaches Dr. Watson on the moor to urge him to leave for London and to take Sir Henry away. When Stapleton appears, she hides what she has done, and later qualifies her warning as fear connected with the Baskerville curse, explaining that Stapleton would be angry if he knew. She also earnestly warns Sir Henry himself to leave the dangerous moor, though Stapleton restrains the development of Sir Henry’s attraction to her. She believes in the hound, unlike Watson. Her apparent role as Stapleton’s sister is exposed as a device: she is his wife, kept seemingly free so that she will be more useful to him. Near the end, she is discovered at Merripit House bound to a beam, gagged, bruised, and tortured. She tells Holmes of Stapleton’s intended refuge, then eagerly guides Holmes and Watson along Stapleton’s track through the bog, her relief revealing the horror of her life with him.

l: Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Selden is an escaped convict from Princetown, identified as the Notting Hill murderer, whose ferocity and brutality make him feared by local farmers and pursued by warders. Desperate and believed capable of stopping at nothing, he hides on the moor, though residents later think he has left after no sightings. He is Eliza Barrymore’s younger brother, and Barrymore secretly supplies him with food and provisions. Watson and Sir Henry discover him through his signal light, but he escapes by throwing a rock and outrunning them. Selden says another man is also concealed on the moor and supplied by a boy. He plans to travel to South America once arrangements are made. During his escape, he wears Sir Henry’s clothing; the hound tracks him, and he falls over rocks, breaks his neck, and is found dead on the moor.

l: the Baskerville legend, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: concerns the moor [warning against nighttime travel] The Baskerville legend is described as a queer old legend that Dr. Mortimer has read to Sherlock Holmes and the others. Holmes reminds Sir Henry of its warning to avoid the moor during the dark hours when the powers of evil are exalted.

l: the persecution of Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: is_not_caused_by James Desmond [according to Sherlock Holmes] Sherlock Holmes considers whether James Desmond, the next heir, could be responsible for the persecution of Sir Henry Baskerville. He concludes that Desmond’s amiable disposition makes this unlikely and says that Desmond can be eliminated from consideration.

l: Selden's prison escape, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Selden’s prison escape began at Princetown, leaving him at large for three days as warders watched roads and stations and farmers feared him. Seeking help from the Barrymores, he reached Baskerville Hall, then hid on the moor until the pursuit passed.

l: the train journey to Devonshire, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The train journey to Devonshire is swift and pleasant. Dr. Watson becomes better acquainted with Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Mortimer, while Sir Henry watches the changing countryside and eagerly recognizes the Devon scenery. During the journey, Dr. Mortimer points out the first sight of the moor.

l: the woman crying in Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: is_a woman [heard sobbing in the house at night] The woman crying in Baskerville Hall is heard by Dr. Watson in the middle of the night. He identifies the sound as a woman’s sob, a muffled and strangling gasp caused by uncontrollable sorrow. He believes the sound is inside the house and not far away, but hears nothing further for half an hour.

l: Grimpen Mire, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Grimpen Mire, also called the Great Grimpen Mire, is a huge, fog-covered moorland bog and morass, foul, deceptive, and dangerous to cross. Its quagmires, slime, hidden depths, and apparently safe green patches can swallow moor ponies or people; one pony disappears and dies, and another seems to be swallowed before Watson and Jack. The cry on the moor is believed to have come from its direction or borders. Jack says he can reach isolated places by following complex landmarks, but warns that entering without a guide is almost certainly fatal. Beyond its bog lies an island of refuge, containing an old tin mine that may be Stapleton’s refuge. Dense fog later conceals the mire and hinders pursuit. Stapleton uses his knowledge of its marked path, learned during insect hunts, to hide and kennel the hound; Anthony likely tends it. The mire may finally bury Stapleton permanently.

l: the Hound's cry, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: is_attributed_to the Baskerville hound [by the peasants] A long, mournful cry rises over the moor while Dr. Watson and Jack Stapleton are walking. The peasants identify it as the Hound of the Baskervilles calling for its prey, while Jack proposes that it may have been caused by bogs or the cry of a rare bittern.

l: bleak moorland house, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: A former prosperous grazier's farm, repaired into a modern dwelling, stands amid a stunted orchard and moor, appearing mean and melancholy outside but containing large, elegantly furnished rooms.

l: warning to Sir Henry, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: concerns danger to Sir Henry [a warning to leave the place of danger] Beryl's warning tells Sir Henry to leave the moor and avoid the place that has supposedly been fatal to his family. She later tells Watson that she has done her duty but cannot give any definite information about the danger.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The Hound of the Baskervilles is a supposed family ghost in the Baskerville curse, feared by Beryl but dismissed by Dr. Watson. It is actually a strong, half-starved savage dog, hidden in a Grimpen Mire kennel and made terrifying with phosphorus paint by Stapleton. Stapleton uses it to pursue Sir Charles and plans it for Sir Henry, but Holmes and Watson kill it when it attacks Sir Henry.

l: the stone huts, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The stone huts are hundreds of abandoned structures on the hillside and moor. One has been used as a habitation, containing blankets, a fire, cooking utensils, water, food tins, spirits, and provisions. Believed to hold the lurking man, they become the narrator’s next focus after questions about Mrs. Laura Lyons remain unresolved.

l: the letters to Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: record Dr. John Watson [his feelings and suspicions at the time] Watson’s letters to Mr. Sherlock Holmes record events and preserve his feelings and suspicions more accurately than memory. One page is missing, but the remaining letters are described as exactly written.

l: the reports to Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Watson’s previous letters and telegrams have kept Mr. Sherlock Holmes informed about events at Baskerville Hall. Watson says that he had little important to report until the surprising events described in this unit and promises that his next report will explain the plan of campaign.

l: Barrymore's secret nighttime vigil, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Barrymore’s secret nighttime vigil is a nocturnal watch at Baskerville Hall. He leaves his room with a candle, enters an unoccupied room, and holds the light at a western window toward the moor with rigid expectation. After groaning, he extinguishes it and returns; Watson hears a key turn, while Sir Henry and Dr. Watson plan to follow him.

l: the Stapleton–Sir Henry courtship, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: exists_between Sir Henry Baskerville [with Miss Stapleton] Sir Henry Baskerville and Miss Stapleton appear mutually attracted after their first meeting. Jack Stapleton repeatedly prevents them from being alone and shows disapproval, despite the apparent advantages of their possible marriage.

l: the old wardrobe (Sir Henry's), The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: is_passed_on_by Barrymore [to aid Selden's escape] Sir Henry Baskerville’s old wardrobe had been given to Barrymore, who passed it on to Selden to help him escape. Selden was wearing Sir Henry’s boots, shirt, cap, and other clothing when he died, and Holmes believes the hound followed the scent of one of these items.

l: the Barrymores' nighttime signal, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The Barrymores’ nighttime signal is a candle held by John Barrymore at the western lattice window of Baskerville Hall. He waits for Selden’s answering light on the moor; together the lights confirm Selden remains there and direct food to him.

l: the plan of campaign, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: is_created_by Dr. John Watson [with Sir Henry Baskerville, based on observations of Barrymore] Watson and Sir Henry Baskerville create a plan of campaign based on Watson’s observations of Barrymore’s nighttime behavior. Watson does not yet reveal its details, reserving them for a later report.

l: Sir Henry and Miss Stapleton's meeting, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Sir Henry and Miss Stapleton privately meet on the moor path; she warns him of danger before Stapleton angrily interrupts, observes them, and leads her away.

l: Sir Henry's proposal to Miss Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Sir Henry tells Miss Stapleton that he loves her and proposes that she marry him. Before she can answer, Stapleton arrives and objects angrily to Sir Henry’s attentions.

l: Stapleton's confrontation with Sir Henry, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: is_caused_by Sir Henry's proposal to Miss Stapleton [and his private meeting with her] Stapleton confronts Sir Henry after seeing him with Miss Stapleton and demands to know why he is paying her attentions. The confrontation becomes angry, but Stapleton later apologizes and withdraws his opposition temporarily.

l: romantic love and marriage, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: is_desired_by Sir Henry Baskerville [with Miss Stapleton] Sir Henry is strongly infatuated with Miss Stapleton and believes that she returns his feelings. He proposes marriage, but Stapleton’s opposition and Miss Stapleton’s warnings prevent an immediate answer, and Sir Henry agrees to postpone the matter for three months.

l: the Barrymores' secret assistance to Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The Barrymores secretly aid Selden with food, shelter, and care because Eliza cannot abandon her younger brother; after he hides on the moor, they use a nighttime signal to check on him and keep sending food, hoping he leaves.

l: the cry on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: is_identified_as the Hound of the Baskervilles [according to local people] The cry on the moor rises from a deep mutter into a howl and ends in a sad moan. Sir Henry identifies it as the cry of a hound, while Watson can only say that its source is uncertain.

l: the mysterious tall man on the tor, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The mysterious tall man on the tor is an unidentified tall, thin person, distinct from Selden. Watson sees him silhouetted against the moon on a granite tor, arms folded and head bowed; he vanishes when Watson turns to Sir Henry, who suggests he may be a warder.

l: Mrs. Laura Lyons, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Mrs. Laura Lyons is a woman living in Coombe Tracey, the estranged daughter of Frankland, and the owner of a typewriting business established with local assistance. In an unhappy, persecuting marriage, she seeks freedom through a projected divorce and is largely supported by Sir Charles Baskerville’s kindness, as well as assistance from Stapleton. She corresponds with and has met Sir Charles, writing him a letter requesting help with divorce-related expenses. Her letter asks him to meet her at the gate on the day of his death, connecting her to the murder inquiry. Initially she denies writing it, then says she did not attend because help came from another source. She is involved intimately with Jack Stapleton and expects to marry him, believing him unmarried. Stapleton manipulates her: he dictates the letter, claims money is needed for her divorce, promises marriage, prevents her from keeping the appointment, conceals that he is married, and threatens her into silence. Once the truth is made clear, she admits Stapleton’s role and agrees to reveal what she knows, helping clarify the affair surrounding Sir Charles’s death.

l: the lurking man on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: The entity is a secret stranger, a tall, thin, apparently gentlemanly man lurking on the moor. He hides and lives in abandoned stone huts on the hillside, with Spartan habits and little concern for comfort. Others watch for and seek him after Selden reports seeing him among the huts. He is supplied with food by a boy who serves as his helper and messenger. While Watson first sees him watching from a tor and investigators try to locate him, the stranger has Watson observed through an agent. In the end, he comes to the hut and speaks to Watson.

l: Coombe Tracey, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Coombe Tracey is a destination and the home of Mrs. Laura Lyons. A letter signed L. L. is sent from there, and a hidden stranger may obtain supplies there. Dr. John Watson goes there to interview Lyons, whose centrally located, well-appointed rooms make her a possible source of assistance in the case; his trip is later noted in a written report.

l: Black Tor, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: Black Tor is a summit on the moor, where Watson saw the stranger; pointed out by Mr. Frankland as a stony hill, it becomes the centre of Watson’s search.

l: the chase of Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: is_a chase [an abortive pursuit on the moor] The chase of Selden has ended without his capture, and Barrymore argues that pursuing him was unfair after the household learned his secret. Sir Henry ultimately agrees not to notify the police while Barrymore arranges for Selden to escape to South America.

l: the blackmailing case, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: is_a complex affair [under investigation] The case concerns the danger surrounding Sir Henry Baskerville and the activities of Jack Stapleton. Sherlock Holmes says that the investigation is nearly complete but requires another day or two and the continued protection of Sir Henry.

l: the appointment between Mrs. Laura Lyons and Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles
s: is_not_kept_by Mrs. Laura Lyons [she says something intervened] Mrs. Laura Lyons arranged to meet Sir Charles Baskerville at the garden gate at ten o’clock on the day he died. She acknowledges making the appointment but denies attending it, saying that something intervened and that she received help from another source.
